concepts.name: Classification of Factors of Production: Traditional vs. Modern Views
key_dimensions: Classical 3-factor model (Land, Labour, Capital) vs. modern 4-factor model adding Entrepreneurship
Emerging debates on Technology/Knowledge as a 5th factor of production
Why Human Capital is sometimes treated separately from Labour
UPSC trap: distinguishing 'factors of production' from 'inputs of production' in exam context

concepts.name: Land as a Factor of Production: Characteristics and Scope
key_dimensions: Broad economic definition of Land (includes all natural resources, not just soil)
Key characteristic: fixed supply at macro level — basis of Ricardian rent theory
Distinction between renewable and non-renewable natural resources within 'Land'
UPSC trap: Land in economics ≠ land in common usage; includes rivers, minerals, sunlight, airspace

concepts.name: Concept of Economic Rent and its Determination
key_dimensions: Ricardo's theory of rent: surplus over cost of production on marginal (no-rent) land
Modern generalization: Economic rent as payment above transfer earnings (applicable to all factors)
Quasi-rent: temporary surplus earned by fixed factors in short run (Marshall's concept)
UPSC trap: difference between 'rent' in common parlance vs. 'economic rent' vs. 'quasi-rent'

concepts.name: Labour as a Factor of Production: Unique Characteristics
key_dimensions: Labour is inseparable from the labourer — implications for labour market functioning
Labour cannot be stored; perishable nature affects wage bargaining
Backward-bending supply curve of labour — when wages rise beyond a point, labour supply falls
UPSC trap: Labour is both a factor of production AND a consumer, creating dual market role

concepts.name: Wages: Types, Theories, and Real vs. Nominal Distinction
key_dimensions: Nominal wage vs. Real wage — relevance to inflation policy and worker welfare
Theories of wages: Subsistence theory, Wage Fund theory, Marginal Productivity theory
Efficiency wages: paying above market rate to boost productivity (modern relevance)
UPSC trap: Minimum wage vs. Living wage vs. Fair wage — three distinct concepts often confused

concepts.name: Capital as a Factor of Production: Types and Distinction from Money
key_dimensions: Capital in economics = produced means of production (NOT money or financial assets)
Fixed capital vs. Circulating (Working) capital — different depreciation and mobility characteristics
Physical capital vs. Human capital vs. Social capital — UPSC frequently tests these distinctions
UPSC trap: Money is NOT capital in economic sense; capital is a real (not financial) concept

concepts.name: Interest as the Return to Capital: Theories and Determinants
key_dimensions: Classical loanable funds theory vs. Keynesian liquidity preference theory of interest
Real interest rate vs. Nominal interest rate (Fisher Effect)
Zero Lower Bound (ZLB) problem and negative interest rates — contemporary relevance
UPSC trap: Interest in economics = return to capital, not merely a banking phenomenon

concepts.name: Entrepreneurship as the Fourth Factor: Role and Reward
key_dimensions: Entrepreneurship: combines other factors, bears risk and uncertainty (Knight's distinction: risk vs. uncertainty)
Schumpeter's 'creative destruction' — entrepreneur as innovator, not just risk-bearer
Profit as the reward for entrepreneurship — residual claimant theory
UPSC trap: Normal profit (implicit cost) vs. Supernormal/Economic profit — only economic profit = true surplus

concepts.name: Mobility of Factors of Production: Geographic and Occupational
key_dimensions: Geographic mobility vs. Occupational mobility — different policy implications
Land has zero geographic mobility but some 'use mobility' (land use change)
Labour mobility barriers: skill mismatch, language, social ties — relevant to Indian labour market
UPSC trap: High mobility of capital (especially financial capital) vs. low mobility of labour — basis of globalization debates

concepts.name: Human Capital: Formation, Measurement, and Policy Relevance
key_dimensions: Human Capital = stock of knowledge, skills, health embodied in individuals (Schultz, Becker)
Sources of human capital formation: education, health, on-the-job training, migration
Human Development Index (HDI) as a partial proxy for human capital stock
UPSC trap: Human capital (economic concept) vs. Human development (broader welfare concept) — frequently tested

concepts.name: Marginal Productivity Theory of Factor Pricing
key_dimensions: Each factor is paid its Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) in a competitive market
MRP = Marginal Physical Product (MPP) × Price of output
Exploitation under monopsony: wage paid < MRP — basis for minimum wage justification
UPSC trap: Theory assumes perfect competition — real markets (monopsony in labour) violate this assumption

concepts.name: Transfer Earnings and Economic Surplus of Factors
key_dimensions: Transfer earnings = minimum payment to keep a factor in its current use (opportunity cost)
Economic surplus = actual earnings minus transfer earnings (generalized rent concept)
Factor with perfectly inelastic supply: entire earning is economic rent (e.g., unique talent)
UPSC trap: All factors earn economic rent to varying degrees — it is NOT exclusive to land

concepts.name: Depreciation and Capital Consumption: Concepts and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Depreciation = wearing out of capital stock over time; reduces productive capacity
Gross Investment vs. Net Investment: Net = Gross minus Depreciation — critical for GDP vs. NDP
Methods of depreciation: Straight-line, Written-down value — different tax and accounting implications
UPSC trap: Capital Consumption Allowance (CCA) in National Accounts — links micro depreciation to macro aggregates

concepts.name: Law of Variable Proportions (Returns to a Factor)
key_dimensions: Short-run law: one factor fixed, other variable — three stages of returns
Stage I: Increasing returns; Stage II: Diminishing returns; Stage III: Negative returns
Rational producer operates in Stage II — basis of optimal factor use decisions
UPSC trap: Returns to a Factor (short run, one factor varies) ≠ Returns to Scale (long run, all factors vary)

concepts.name: Returns to Scale: Constant, Increasing, and Decreasing
key_dimensions: Long-run concept: all factors vary proportionately — tests scale efficiency
Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS): basis for economies of scale and natural monopoly argument
Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS): managerial inefficiency, coordination failures at large scale
UPSC trap: IRS in production ≠ increasing returns to a factor; confusion between short-run and long-run analysis

concepts.name: Factor Substitutability and Complementarity: Production Isoquants
key_dimensions: Isoquant shows combinations of two factors producing same output — convex due to diminishing MRTS
Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS): rate at which one factor replaces another
Perfect substitutes (straight-line isoquant) vs. Perfect complements (L-shaped/Leontief isoquant)
UPSC trap: Capital-Labour substitutability is central to automation/employment debates in Indian policy context

concepts.name: Profit: Normal Profit vs. Economic Profit and their Significance
key_dimensions: Normal profit = implicit cost of entrepreneurship; included in cost curves (zero economic profit condition)
Economic (Supernormal) profit signals resource reallocation in market economies
Sources of profit: innovation (Schumpeter), risk-bearing (Knight), monopoly power
UPSC trap: A firm 'breaking even' in accounting terms may still be earning normal profit in economic terms

concepts.name: Factor Market vs. Product Market: Derived Demand Concept
key_dimensions: Demand for factors is derived demand — it depends on demand for final goods/services
Implication: demand for construction labour rises with rise in real estate demand
Elasticity of derived demand depends on: elasticity of product demand, substitutability of factors
UPSC trap: Factor markets are demand-constrained by product markets — policy to boost labour demand must address product demand first

concepts.name: Disguised Unemployment and Surplus Labour in Agriculture
key_dimensions: Disguised unemployment: marginal productivity of labour = zero or near zero; excess labour in agriculture
Lewis two-sector model: surplus agricultural labour transferred to industrial sector without reducing output
Relevance to Indian structural transformation and labour migration patterns
UPSC trap: Disguised unemployment is NOT the same as underemployment or seasonal unemployment — three distinct concepts

concepts.name: Technology as an Emerging Factor: Total Factor Productivity (TFP)
key_dimensions: TFP measures output growth not explained by growth in labour and capital inputs (Solow residual)
TFP growth driven by technological progress, innovation, institutional quality
India's TFP growth trends — relevance to economic growth debate beyond input accumulation
UPSC trap: TFP is a residual measure — it captures efficiency and technology but also measurement errors; not a direct observable
